name: Aircraft Maintenance
description: Aircraft maintenance combines technical work with the continuing responsibility to keep an aircraft airworthy. In Iran, historical investigation records document distinct maintenance and airworthiness-management approvals, while foreign export restrictions provide a separate constraint on some aircraft support transactions.

seo.title: Aircraft Maintenance in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand aircraft maintenance, continuing airworthiness, historical Iranian approvals, and the evidence needed to assess maintenance capability.

content.heading: Maintenance is also a continuing responsibility
content.content:
The workshop is only one part of aircraft maintenance. The International Civil Aviation Organization, or ICAO, distinguishes the operator’s continuing responsibility for airworthiness from the organizations that perform or control maintenance. Its explanation of Annex 6 requires operators to ensure that aircraft remain airworthy under procedures acceptable to the country where they are registered. Operators must also employ a person or group responsible for ensuring that maintenance follows the maintenance control manual. [s1]

For readers encountering Iran’s aviation industry, this distinction helps interpret claims about technical capability. A report that a company has repaired an aircraft describes an activity; evidence about the organization’s approval, the aircraft concerned, and continuing oversight addresses different questions. ICAO’s guidance discusses operators, approved maintenance organizations, and maintenance control organizations separately. It does not certify any particular Iranian company or establish that a named aircraft is fit to fly. [s1]

content.heading: A documented Iranian distinction
content.content:
An Iranian aircraft accident investigation report concerning a Mahan Air aircraft records that the airline held both a continuing airworthiness management organization approval, abbreviated CAMO, and an approved maintenance organization approval, abbreviated AMO. The report identifies the relevant Iranian frameworks as CAO.IRI Part-M and Part-145 respectively. This provides a historical example of the distinction between managing continuing airworthiness and performing approved maintenance within Iran’s regulatory system. [s2]

The record should be read within its historical scope. An investigation’s description of approvals at the time does not establish their validity in October 2026, their complete technical scope, or the capabilities of other Iranian airlines. It also cannot support a nationwide conclusion about maintenance quality. A current account would require the approval certificates and their scope, together with evidence of subsequent oversight. [s2]

content.heading: Technical approval and international support are separate questions
content.content:
Foreign export controls add another layer. In September 2022, the United States Bureau of Industry and Security identified Iranian-operated cargo aircraft that it alleged had flown to Russia in violation of US export controls. Its notice expressly addressed maintenance, repairs, spare parts, refuelling, and other services involving listed aircraft under the stated legal conditions. [s3]

This notice establishes the US agency’s position and the historical enforcement context. It does not establish that every maintenance transaction involving Iran is prohibited, nor does it measure the technical condition of the aircraft concerned. Treating a trade restriction as a safety inspection would confuse different forms of evidence. Conversely, a domestic technical approval does not itself resolve the separate question of whether an international supplier may lawfully provide a particular service. The current legal position requires updated, transaction-specific documentation. [s3]

The practical reading framework is therefore to ask who manages airworthiness, who performs the work, what approval covers it, and what support restrictions apply. The inspected evidence explains those distinctions but does not yet support a current directory of Iranian maintenance providers. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Airport Management
description: Airport management brings together the operation, maintenance, documentation, and safety coordination of an aerodrome. Iran Airports and Air Navigation Company is documented as a major airport operator, but operator descriptions alone do not establish the safety performance or current certification of individual airports.

seo.title: Airport Management in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s airport operating structure and the distinction between airport management, certification, and demonstrated safety performance.

content.heading: An operating network with several responsibilities
content.content:
An airport is an operating organization as well as a physical site. The Airports Council International Asia-Pacific and Middle East directory identifies Iran Airports and Air Navigation Company as an operator of airports across Iran. Its entry includes Mehrabad in Tehran, Mashhad, Shiraz, Tabriz, Bandar Abbas, and numerous smaller locations. The accompanying organizational description places airport leadership, management, maintenance, development, air navigation, and air traffic management among the company’s duties and describes its affiliation with the Ministry of Roads and Urban Development. [s1]

That description explains institutional scope, rather than demonstrated results. It does not establish that every airport in Iran has the same operator or that every listed facility offers the same services. The directory does not provide a dated airport-by-airport certification register, audited operating results, or a consistent annual performance series. Its network totals therefore should not be treated as verified October 2026 statistics. [s1]

content.heading: Management and certification have different roles
content.content:
ICAO’s aerodrome certification programme distinguishes the work of civil aviation authorities from the work of airport operators. Authorities develop certification rules and undertake certification and oversight; operators need the technical knowledge and procedures to meet the applicable standards. The programme identifies operational procedures, a safety management system, an aerodrome manual, and monitoring processes as central elements of certification. An aerodrome is the operational site used for aircraft arrivals, departures, and movement. [s2]

For readers assessing an Iranian airport, these distinctions make the evidence easier to interpret. A directory entry establishes an operator’s identity. A certificate and its conditions address regulatory authorization. A manual describes operating arrangements, while monitoring addresses continuing compliance. None of these documents alone supplies a complete account of service quality or actual safety outcomes. This is an editorial framework drawn from ICAO’s separation of certification, documentation, and monitoring functions, rather than a finding about any particular Iranian airport. [s2]

content.heading: The organization behind the infrastructure
content.content:
Material presented by Airports Council International at an ICAO certification workshop emphasizes the operator’s organizational capability. Its discussion of on-site verification asks whether management has committed to safety, whether staff responsibilities and reporting lines are defined, and whether the operator monitors training for employees and subcontractors. These are international assessment principles; they are not evidence that a particular Iranian operator has passed an assessment. [s3]

The distinction matters when considering airport development. Buildings and flight surfaces are visible, but an assessment also needs to examine the people and procedures supporting their operation. The workshop material treats management competence, responsibility, and training as subjects for verification. A useful account of airport management must therefore connect physical facilities with documented organizational arrangements, rather than infer effective operation from infrastructure alone. [s3]

Iran’s airport network can be introduced through the operator directory and these international concepts. A publication-ready assessment of its current management still needs dated Iranian certification records, local operating documentation, and evidence of results. [s1][s2][s3]

content.title: An international framework for understanding airport certification
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Civil aviation authority"] -->|"Develops certification rules and conducts oversight"| B["Aerodrome certification process"]
  C["Airport operator"] -->|"Develops operating documentation"| D["Aerodrome manual"]
  C -->|"Implements operational safety arrangements"| E["Safety management system"]
  D -->|"Documentation considered in certification"| B
  E -->|"System considered in certification"| B
  B -->|"Includes monitoring for regulatory compliance"| F["Continuing compliance monitoring"]
```
content.summary: This diagram summarizes ICAO’s general certification framework. It does not depict verified reporting lines in Iran or certify any Iranian airport.

name: Maritime Transport
description: Iran’s maritime transport system combines ports, terminal operations, shipping, and connections to inland transport. Its port network includes southern gateways such as Bandar Abbas and Chabahar and northern ports such as Anzali and Amirabad, with different roles that cannot be captured by a single throughput figure.

seo.title: Maritime Transport in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran’s port network, Chabahar’s documented terminal agreement, historical cargo volumes, and the limits of current evidence.

content.heading: A network of ports and inland connections
content.content:
Maritime transport is broader than the movement of ships. For Iran, the subject includes the institutions responsible for ports, the terminals handling cargo, and the inland connections that allow goods to reach their destinations. The International Association of Ports and Harbors lists Bandar Abbas, Imam Khomeini, Bushehr, Chabahar, Anzali, Noshahr, and Amirabad among ports associated with Iran’s Ports and Maritime Organization, usually abbreviated PMO. Its institutional description identifies maritime commerce, coastal communications, and port-related charges among PMO’s responsibilities. [s1]

This list establishes the breadth of the network, but it is not a ranking of port performance. Nor does inclusion under a national organization mean that every terminal has an identical operating arrangement. The documented Chabahar agreement illustrates why it is useful to distinguish a port authority from the company contracted to equip and operate a particular terminal. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Chabahar: geography, contracts, and corridor ambitions
content.content:
Chabahar faces the Sea of Oman in southeastern Iran, outside the Strait of Hormuz. A field-based study by the Middle East Institute of Japan explains its significance as an alternative maritime gateway and as part of efforts to connect Iran with Afghanistan, Central Asia, and wider regional markets. The same study describes the International North-South Transport Corridor as a multimodal route linking India and Russia through Iran, the Caucasus, and the Caspian Sea. These are overlapping connectivity ambitions rather than proof of a single seamless transport service. [s3]

On 13 May 2024, India Ports Global Limited and Iran’s PMO signed a long-term contract concerning the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar. India’s official announcement identifies the parties and the terminal. A subsequent parliamentary statement describes a ten-year arrangement to equip and operate its general cargo and container terminal. These records support a specific contractual development; they do not establish completion of every proposed port or inland transport investment. [s2][s4]

That distinction is important for rail connectivity. The Japanese institute’s study reported that the Chabahar–Zahedan railway remained incomplete in late February 2024. This is a dated observation, not a statement of its October 2026 condition. It demonstrates why a map of intended corridors needs to distinguish existing transport links from infrastructure still being developed at the time of observation. [s3]

content.heading: What the available cargo figures establish
content.content:
An Indian parliamentary answer published in March 2025 reports cargo volumes for Shahid Beheshti at Chabahar. The four completed fiscal-year entries retained below show higher reported volume in FY 2023–24 than in FY 2020–21, with a small decline between FY 2021–22 and FY 2022–23. These figures concern the named facility in that answer. They are not Iran’s national maritime trade, a measure of all Chabahar terminals, or a container-only series. [s5]

The answer also lists FY 2024–25, but it was issued before that Indian financial year ended. The cargo table does not specify the final observation date. That entry is therefore excluded from the comparable completed-year series. The source does not explain its cargo-counting methodology sufficiently to determine whether categories such as transshipment or empty equipment are included. These limits matter before comparing its figures with other port publications. [s5]

content.title: Reported cargo volume at Shahid Beheshti, Chabahar
content.interpretation: Reported cargo volume rose between FY 2020–21 and FY 2023–24, with a small decline in FY 2022–23. This facility-specific series does not establish a national trend or explain the causes of the changes.

content.heading: Assessing development without confusing plans and results
content.content:
A sound reading of Iran’s maritime development separates institutional responsibilities, terminal contracts, physical connections, and measured cargo movements. A contract records an agreed operating framework. A cargo observation records activity within a defined reporting period. A corridor study explains strategic possibilities and constraints. None alone establishes the cost, reliability, or present availability of a complete shipping route. [s1][s2][s3][s5]

The evidence assembled here offers a historical introduction and a limited facility-level trend. A current national overview still requires comparable statistics for the other major ports, verified shipping services, and updated evidence about inland connections and operational disruptions. The individual port pages provide the appropriate structure for that further research, while container shipping requires separate measures from cargo tonnage.
